value: Ability differences within an already-selected group of STEM undergraduates, and which of those differences predict which first-year grades.

Does spatial visualisation ability predict first-year achievements in advanced STEM courses beyond numerical and verbal reasoning, and does its predictive validity differ between math-intensive and explicitly spatial subjects?

In 317 first-year STEM undergraduates, spatial visualisation uniquely predicted grades only in an explicitly spatial technical-drawing course, while numerical and verbal reasoning predicted math and physics grades, indicating a narrower role for spatial ability in math-intensive advanced learning.

quote: In a prospective cohort design, we assessed students from two STEM programs on multiple measures of SV, numerical and verbal reasoning abilities.
Math and physics achievements were best predicted by numerical, verbal and general reasoning abilities.

Advanced mathematics is carried out by translating spatial structures into abstract symbolic formalism rather than by visualizing them, so exceptional visualization ability adds nothing to math achievement
quote: Math courses may focus on translating complex spatial structures into abstract mathematical formalism, more than they require superb visualization of such structures.

value: Where spatial tests do correlate with math grades, the link runs through domain-general reasoning components embedded in those tests rather than through visualization itself
quote: Additionally, our finding that positive correlations between one type of SV tests (visualization of cross-sections) and some math achievements were mediated by factors common to other domains of reasoning suggests that factors other than visualization—which may be strongly present in some spatial tests—play a role when it comes to mathematics.

Very broadly, spatial ability (SA) refers to “the ability to generate, retain, and manipulate abstract visual images” [ 19 ].

The most studied type of SA in the context of STEM is spatial visualization (SV), which is the ability to “…apprehend a spatial form, shape or scene in order to match it with another spatial form, shape or scene, often with the necessity of rotating it in two or three dimensions one or more times” [ 24 ].
